blocks.body:
Can finitely many arithmetic progressions, all with different common differences, cover every integer? With differences $2$ and $2$ it is trivial (evens and odds), but if the moduli must be distinct it is a genuine puzzle. Here is a solution:
$$0 \bmod 2,\quad 0 \bmod 3,\quad 1 \bmod 4,\quad 5 \bmod 6,\quad 7 \bmod 12.$$
Erdős introduced such systems in 1950 to build integers with surprising arithmetic properties, and asked many questions about them. This lesson explains how to check a covering, proves the basic density facts (including the theorem that an exact covering cannot have distinct moduli), shows how coverings produce Sierpiński numbers, and describes Hough's 2015 solution of the minimum modulus problem.

blocks.title: Covering system
blocks.body:
A covering system is a finite collection of residue classes $a_1 \bmod n_1, \dots, a_k \bmod n_k$ with all $n_i \ge 2$ such that
$$\bigcup_{i=1}^{k} \{x \in \mathbb{Z} : x \equiv a_i \pmod{n_i}\} = \mathbb{Z}.$$
It has distinct moduli if $n_1 < n_2 < \cdots < n_k$, and it is exact if every integer lies in exactly one of the classes.

Requiring $n_i \ge 2$ rules out the trivial covering by the single class $0 \bmod 1$.

blocks.title: Checking a covering
blocks.body:
A class $a \bmod n$ is periodic with period $n$, so the union of the classes is periodic with period $L = \operatorname{lcm}(n_1, \dots, n_k)$. Hence a system covers $\mathbb{Z}$ if and only if it covers $0, 1, \dots, L-1$. (Equivalently, by the [[crt|Chinese remainder theorem]], each class $a_i \bmod n_i$ is a union of $L/n_i$ classes modulo $L$, and we need all $L$ classes.)

For the system in the introduction $L = 12$, and the classes modulo $12$ are:
- $0 \bmod 2$: $0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10$
- $0 \bmod 3$: $0, 3, 6, 9$
- $1 \bmod 4$: $1, 5, 9$
- $5 \bmod 6$: $5, 11$
- $7 \bmod 12$: $7$

Every residue from $0$ to $11$ appears, so this is a covering with distinct moduli. A computer search over all smaller values confirms that $12$ is the least possible $L$ for a covering with distinct moduli.

There is also a quick necessary condition. Within one period of length $L$, the class $a_i \bmod n_i$ contains exactly $L/n_i$ integers. If the classes cover all $L$ integers, then
$$\sum_{i=1}^{k} \frac{L}{n_i} \ge L,\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad \sum_{i=1}^{k} \frac{1}{n_i} \ge 1,$$
with equality exactly when no integer is covered twice, i.e. when the covering is exact. In the example, $\frac12+\frac13+\frac14+\frac16+\frac1{12} = \frac{16}{12}$, so there is overlap ($0$, $6$ and $9$ are hit twice, for instance).

blocks.title: Reciprocal sum is not enough
blocks.body: The moduli $2, 3, 4$ have $\frac12+\frac13+\frac14 = \frac{13}{12} > 1$. Show that nevertheless no choice of $a \bmod 2$, $b \bmod 3$, $c \bmod 4$ covers $\mathbb{Z}$.
blocks.solution:
Work modulo $4$ first. The class $a \bmod 2$ covers two of the four residues modulo $4$, and $c \bmod 4$ covers one.

If $c \equiv a \pmod 2$, the class $c \bmod 4$ lies inside $a \bmod 2$, so together they cover only the two residues of one parity modulo $4$. The other parity class, a full class modulo $2$, is left, and $b \bmod 3$ meets it only in one class modulo $6$, leaving two of its three residues modulo $6$ uncovered.

If $c \not\equiv a \pmod 2$, the two classes cover three residues modulo $4$, and one class $d \bmod 4$ is uncovered. The class $b \bmod 3$ meets $d \bmod 4$ in exactly one class modulo $12$ (by the Chinese remainder theorem), so the other two classes modulo $12$ inside $d \bmod 4$ are uncovered.

Either way some integer is missed. The point: two of the moduli share the factor $2$, so the classes overlap in a forced way, and the reciprocal sum overestimates what they can cover. Covering problems are about this interplay between overlaps and the arithmetic of the moduli.

blocks.title: Exact coverings cannot have distinct moduli
blocks.body: The covering $0 \bmod 2,\ 1 \bmod 4,\ 3 \bmod 4$ is exact, and its largest modulus $4$ appears twice. That is no accident. The next theorem, found independently around 1950 by Davenport, Mirsky, Newman and Rado (and often called the Mirsky–Newman theorem), says the largest modulus of an exact covering always repeats. Combined with the density count above, it implies that a covering with distinct moduli always has $\sum 1/n_i > 1$.

blocks.title: Mirsky–Newman theorem
blocks.body: Let $a_i \bmod n_i$ ($1 \le i \le k$, all $n_i \ge 2$) be an exact covering of $\mathbb{Z}$. Then the largest modulus $\max_i n_i$ occurs at least twice. In particular, an exact covering cannot have distinct moduli, and every covering with distinct moduli satisfies $\sum_i 1/n_i > 1$.

blocks.title: Proof by generating functions
blocks.body:
We may take $0 \le a_i < n_i$. Exactness means every integer $m \ge 0$ can be written in exactly one way as $m = a_i + j n_i$ with $1 \le i \le k$ and $j \ge 0$. For a complex number $z$ with $|z| < 1$, sum $z^m$ over all $m \ge 0$ in two ways:
$$\sum_{i=1}^{k} \frac{z^{a_i}}{1 - z^{n_i}} = \sum_{i=1}^{k}\sum_{j \ge 0} z^{a_i + j n_i} = \sum_{m \ge 0} z^m = \frac{1}{1-z}.$$

Suppose the largest modulus $N = n_k$ occurs only once, so $n_i < N$ for $i < k$. Let $\zeta = e^{2\pi i/N}$, a primitive $N$-th root of unity, and let $z = t\zeta$ with $0 < t < 1$, $t \to 1$.

- For $i < k$: $0 < n_i < N$, so $N \nmid n_i$ and $\zeta^{n_i} \ne 1$. Thus $1 - z^{n_i} \to 1 - \zeta^{n_i} \ne 0$ and the $i$-th term stays bounded.
- The right side: $\zeta \ne 1$ because $N \ge 2$, so $\frac{1}{1-z} \to \frac{1}{1-\zeta}$ stays bounded.
- The $k$-th term: $z^{N} = t^{N}$, so $\left|\frac{z^{a_k}}{1-z^{N}}\right| = \frac{t^{a_k}}{1 - t^{N}} \to \infty$.

The identity then says an unbounded quantity equals a bounded one, a contradiction. So $N$ occurs at least twice.

For the last statement: a covering always has $\sum 1/n_i \ge 1$, with equality only if it is exact; an exact covering cannot have distinct moduli, so with distinct moduli the inequality is strict.

blocks.title: Erdős's application and Sierpiński numbers
blocks.body:
Coverings are useful because they turn into divisibility. Suppose $p$ is a prime with $\operatorname{ord}_p(2) = n$ (see [[order-primroot]]). Then $2^m \bmod p$ depends only on $m \bmod n$. If we can arrange that some quantity built from $2^m$ is divisible by $p$ whenever $m \equiv a \pmod n$, then a covering system $a_i \bmod n_i$, with a different prime $p_i$ of order $n_i$ for each class, forces divisibility by some $p_i$ for every $m$.

Erdős (1950) used the covering
$$0 \bmod 2,\ 0 \bmod 3,\ 1 \bmod 4,\ 3 \bmod 8,\ 7 \bmod 12,\ 23 \bmod 24$$
with the primes $3, 7, 5, 17, 13, 241$, whose orders of $2$ are $2, 3, 4, 8, 12, 24$ respectively (all six divide $2^{24} - 1$). By the Chinese remainder theorem choose odd $N$ with $N \equiv 2^{a_i} \pmod{p_i}$ for each class. Then for every $k \ge 0$, $k$ lies in some class $a_i \bmod n_i$, so $2^k \equiv 2^{a_i} \equiv N \pmod{p_i}$ and $p_i \mid N - 2^k$. Hence $N - 2^k$ is never prime unless it equals one of the six primes. This gives a whole residue class of odd $N$ that are almost never of the form $2^k + p$; discarding the sparse set of $N$ for which some $N - p_i$ is a power of $2$, Erdős obtained a positive proportion of odd numbers not of the form $2^k + p$. The smallest positive $N$ in his residue class is $7629217$.

Sierpiński (1960) applied the same idea to $k\cdot 2^n + 1$. An odd $k$ is a Sierpiński number if $k \cdot 2^n + 1$ is composite for every $n \ge 1$. Coverings show that infinitely many exist. The smallest known one, found by Selfridge in 1962, is $78557$; it is conjectured to be the smallest. Proving this means finding a prime of the form $k \cdot 2^n + 1$ for every smaller odd $k$; large distributed computer searches have done so for all but a handful of them, and those remaining cases are still open.

blocks.title: Why 78557 is a Sierpiński number
blocks.body: Use the primes $3, 5, 7, 13, 19, 37, 73$ to show that $78557 \cdot 2^n + 1$ is composite for every $n \ge 1$.
blocks.solution:
The orders of $2$ modulo these primes are
$$\operatorname{ord}_3 2 = 2,\ \operatorname{ord}_5 2 = 4,\ \operatorname{ord}_7 2 = 3,\ \operatorname{ord}_{13} 2 = 12,\ \operatorname{ord}_{19} 2 = 18,\ \operatorname{ord}_{37} 2 = 36,\ \operatorname{ord}_{73} 2 = 9.$$
For each prime $p$ we solve $78557\cdot 2^n \equiv -1 \pmod p$ for $n$ modulo $\operatorname{ord}_p 2$. A short computation gives one class for each prime:
$$n \equiv 0 \bmod 2\ (p = 3),\quad 1 \bmod 4\ (5),\quad 1 \bmod 3\ (7),\quad 11 \bmod 12\ (13),$$
$$15 \bmod 18\ (19),\quad 27 \bmod 36\ (37),\quad 3 \bmod 9\ (73).$$
For example, modulo $3$ we have $78557 \equiv 2$, and $2 \cdot 2^n + 1 \equiv 0 \pmod 3$ iff $2^{n+1} \equiv 2$ iff $n$ is even.

These seven classes form a covering system (with lcm $36$, check the residues $0, \dots, 35$). So for every $n$, the number $78557\cdot 2^n + 1$ is divisible by one of the seven primes. It exceeds $73$ for every $n \ge 1$, so it is composite.

blocks.title: The minimum modulus problem
blocks.body:
In a covering with distinct moduli, how large can the smallest modulus $n_1$ be? The example above has $n_1 = 2$. Coverings with distinct moduli and $n_1 = 3$, $4$, and larger are known; the constructions get very complicated, and Nielsen (2009) gave one with least modulus $40$. Erdős asked whether $n_1$ can be arbitrarily large.

Hough (2015) answered no: there is an absolute constant $B$ such that every covering system with distinct moduli has least modulus at most $B$, and his argument gives $B \le 10^{16}$. His proof is probabilistic in spirit. Roughly, one treats the classes with moduli built from small primes first and then larger ones, and shows, using a quantitative variant of the Lovász local lemma from the [[probabilistic-method]], that if all moduli are large the classes overlap too much to cover everything. Balister, Bollobás, Morris, Sahasrabudhe and Tiba later found a simpler and more flexible version of the method and improved the constant substantially.

The most famous question that remains open is the Erdős–Selfridge problem: is there a covering system with distinct odd moduli? Several restricted versions (with extra conditions on the prime factors of the moduli) have been settled by refinements of Hough's method; the odd-moduli question itself has not.

Heuristically, odd moduli are hard to use because the cheap modulus $2$, which covers half of everything, is unavailable, while the density condition $\sum 1/n_i > 1$ is easy to meet (the sum of $1/n$ over odd $n$ diverges). The obstruction, if there is one, must come from overlaps, exactly the phenomenon seen in the example with moduli $2,3,4$.

- $\sum 1/n_i \ge 1$ is necessary but far from sufficient: overlaps between classes with non-coprime moduli waste coverage.
- To check a covering you only need residues modulo the lcm, but you need all of them; checking a few hundred integers is not a proof unless that range contains a full period.
- In applications such as Sierpiński numbers, each class needs its own prime, and the number must be larger than that prime to be composite.
- The Mirsky–Newman theorem is about exact coverings; ordinary coverings with distinct moduli exist (the one above).

Covering systems are built from the [[crt|Chinese remainder theorem]] and studied with the counting and probabilistic tools of [[combinatorial-nt]] and the [[probabilistic-method]]. Their applications use [[order-primroot|orders of 2 modulo primes]] and divisibility, and they give elementary obstructions in questions about [[prime-patterns|primes in sequences]]: they explain why some sequences like $k\cdot 2^n + 1$ contain no primes at all, while heuristics would otherwise predict infinitely many.

1. Verify that $$0 \bmod 2,\ 0 \bmod 3,\ 1 \bmod 4,\ 3 \bmod 8,\ 7 \bmod 12,\ 23 \bmod 24$$ covers $\mathbb{Z}$, and compute $\sum 1/n_i$.
2. Show that the moduli $2, 3, 4, 6$ alone (one class each) cannot cover $\mathbb{Z}$, so the class $7 \bmod 12$ in the introduction cannot simply be dropped.
3. Find an exact covering with moduli $2, 4, 8, 8$, and explain why no exact covering has moduli $2, 3, 6$ even though $\frac12+\frac13+\frac16 = 1$.
4. Using the primes $3, 5, 17, 257, 641, 65537, 6700417$, which divide $2^{64} - 1$, explain how a covering with moduli dividing $64$ could be used to produce a Sierpiński-type number. (You need not finish the computation.)
